findings.where: the fourth note down, 'sending you the roster', and the long-press menu behind it
findings.what: A message the far phone refuses is a dead end: the row reads 'it would not go x' in red and there is no way to send it again — the note menu offers only reply, react, edit and delete (app/lib/regions/chat/chat_region.dart:699-723), and app/lib/spine/spine.dart:159 removes refused ids from `pushable` permanently ('it stays out of the wire'), so the outbox will never try again.
findings.why: The row forbids dropped messages; from the couple's side a note they wrote, that will not go and cannot be made to go from inside the app, is a dropped message they have to retype somewhere else. It is not an exotic case: one of the host's two refusal reasons (app/lib/transport/protocol/server_io.dart:238) is a pairing mismatch, which is exactly the condition a person would fix and then want to retry.

findings.where: the whole frame — an empty Chromium window at about:blank on a black desktop
findings.what: Nothing in the evidence shows a message announcing itself while the app is closed. The scene pushed three times to a closed app and logs/reception.json records `records: []`; crops/reception.png and crops/reception_replaced.png are byte-identical (sha256 4677957956d2526f...), so the 'a second notice replaces the first' case is literally the same empty desktop as the first, and no banner appears in either. The log itself says 'there is no lock screen in evidence, and what an installed iOS web app does with the same call is not shown anywhere in this build.'
findings.why: A message that arrives and never tells anyone is the plainest reason either person keeps Instagram installed. RFC 8291 encryption and a VAPID header are proved in logs/webpush.txt and a service worker is registered in logs/pwa.json, but a notification actually appearing is proved nowhere, on any browser.

findings.where: the whole fling — seven throws at -3000 logical px/s over 4.8 s of app time
findings.what: The only measurement in the evidence that bears on real-time cost says roughly a quarter of frames are two orders of magnitude over budget in build alone. logs/scroll_webkit.json: 777 frames, `over_16ms: 777`; build_ms p50 5, p75 43, p90 730, p95 773, max 1109; 187 of 777 frames over 100 ms, arriving every 3 to 6 frames and spread evenly across the session (49, 48, 49, 41 per 200 frames). Raster (p50 117, max 200) is discountable on a headless WebKit with no GPU, but buildDuration is CPU layout and paint-record, and the 3-to-6-frame period matches the rate at which a new row enters a 780 px viewport at ~34 logical px a frame, so the cost is per row of the seeded year.
findings.why: The row forbids scroll jank against the year-deep history, and the clip cannot answer the charge: the clock is driven, one frame per harness step, so no frame can be dropped by construction — I measured all 299 transitions and every one moved exactly what the fling asked (mean error -0.014 device px, sd 0.36, max 0.85). Nothing anywhere in the set shows this thread scrolling in real time on any device, and the one number that speaks to it is bad.

findings.where: the composer, and the margin lines under the five notes
findings.what: The artifact whose job is to show messenger states shows three of five and loses the one it explicitly waited for. Its own script (evidence/scenes/13_messenger_states.json) ends `awaitView partner_typing=true` then `shot`; logs/13_messenger_states.json records `{"awaited":"partner_typing","want":true,"got":true}` and then, read at the shutter, `"partner_typing": false` — the typing indication expired during the 9111 ms awaitView plus 3981 ms shot. `states_on_the_glass` is `{read:1, sent:2, "it would not go":1}`: neither `waiting to send` nor `going` (app/lib/spine/projections/thread.dart:12-27) appears in any artifact. DIFF.json also puts this file at ssim 0.7088 against the previous run of the same scene on a bundle that never changed (app/build/web is entirely 18:47-18:48 and nothing under it was rewritten afterwards), so the scene is not reproducible run to run.
findings.why: The row names delivery state and typing indication, and correct ordering after going offline and reconnecting. The offline path is asserted only in reliability.json (26 events queued, all delivered, seq 1..173 gapless) and never shown; typing is shown, but by accident in two other clips rather than in the artifact built for it.

findings.where: the fixed 'search' chip at the top right, over the thread
findings.what: The search control is opaque paper pinned over the message list and it covers words. Measured over all 300 frames of 11_chat_scroll.mp4: in 220 frames a note's paper lies immediately left of the chip; in 91 of those, dark handwriting runs right up to its left edge, and in a further 80 a light state line does — 171 of 300 frames (57 per cent) with thread content running under it. Two confirmations by eye: the last frame of 06_unfolding.mp4 reads 'sending you th' with the final letter of 'the' behind the chip, and frame 40 of 11_chat_scroll.mp4 has the chip swallowing a state line's timestamp entirely ('Fri 2...').
findings.why: Messages and their times being unreadable more than half the time you scroll is a defect in the messenger's main surface, and it is the kind of small daily friction the row says decides whether they leave Instagram.

findings.where: every voice-note card in the gallery — six of them, at 0:58, 0:31, 1:03, 0:41, 1:58 and 0:52
findings.what: Each reads 'teo .' or 'noor .' — author, separator, and nothing after it. The date is missing and the separator that should introduce it is still drawn. Root cause is checkable: app/lib/regions/moments/moments_region.dart:542 passes `event.ts`, an `int` (app/lib/spine/event.dart:46), to `dayLabel`, which returns '' for anything that is not a `String` (app/lib/thread/note_body.dart:50-53). It is the only bad call site of the three.
findings.why: In a year-deep archive an undated voice note cannot be placed, and the dangling middot is a label printed for a value that is not there — visible evidence that a field is silently empty rather than absent.

findings.where: the scene record, not the frame
findings.what: The only console error in the whole capture. logs/14_media_viewer.json carries `problems: ["console: Failed to load resource: the server responded with a status of 401 (Unauthorized)"]` and `ok: false`. 401 is what app/lib/transport/protocol/server_io.dart:101 returns for an unsigned or unpaired request, and app/lib/transport/protocol/http_transport.dart:209 flips the link to `LinkState.error` on one.
findings.why: The picture itself is fine — the video is playing at position_ms 921 of 2500 with a working scrubber, and the report at the shutter shows the link connected with last_error null — but the media viewer is the one scene the capture marked not-ok, and an unauthorised request against the paired host is exactly the class of fault that loses a photograph on a bad day.

findings.what: A first launch that imports the year takes 8834 ms (13_messenger_states), 10002 ms (01_pulse), 9756 ms (dusk_pulse) and 25878 ms (07_feeling_landing); a phone that already has it opens in 2136-2632 ms. No artifact shows what is on screen during those seconds.
findings.why: The row forbids a spinner that outstays its welcome, and the case where it would most obviously outstay it — up to 26 seconds on the very first launch, in front of a person who has just been told to add this to their home screen — is the one case with no picture at all.

findings.where: the ten hits under the query 'rain', and the 'photographs' and 'video' filter chips above them
findings.what: Media search is offered but not shown. logs/12_search.json records `hits: 10`, `kinds: {message: 8, ritual_kept: 1, todo_event: 1}` — not one photo, video or voice note among the results, and no thumbnail appears anywhere in the frame. The nine-query record in reliability.json (photo, video, voice_note each answered by an event of that type) is a log, not a picture. Separately, no artifact shows a sent reply rendered in the thread: the `_ReplyStrip` exists (app/lib/regions/chat/note.dart:106) and 13_messenger_states.png shows a reply being composed, but the seeded year has only 111 reply_to among 14,061 events, so none landed in an eight-row window.
findings.why: The row names full-text and media search and replies; both are implemented and both go unseen, so a reader of the evidence alone has to take the log's word for two of the twelve named capabilities.

what_is_working: The scroll against the year-deep history is geometrically exact. I cross-correlated all 300 frames of 11_chat_scroll.mp4 against logs/11_chat_scroll.fling.json: every one of the 299 transitions moved what the fling asked for, mean error -0.014 device px, sd 0.36, worst 0.85; smallest step 31 device px, largest 143; no frame repeated, no step backwards, 8455 logical px over 4.8 s of app time across seven throws at -3000 px/s on Flutter's own clamping physics. The fling log's own `moved` equals `asked` to the last decimal on all 300 rows.

Every capability the row names is present somewhere in the evidence: text (02, 13), photographs (04; a fully decoded photograph mid-fling at 11_chat_scroll frame 60), video (14, playing, scrubber at 0:01/0:03; play marks in 04), voice notes (02 at 0:26 with a waveform and 'read' double tick; six in 04; hold-to-record on the composer's three-stroke mark, app/lib/regions/chat/chat_region.dart:1089-1101, which turns red while recording), reactions (a folded object on the first note of 02, `reactions` count 1 in both the 02 and 13 reports), replies (composer reply strip in 13), delivery and read state (13: read, sent x2, refused), typing ('noor writing...' in every strip frame of 11 and 06), editing ('edited' in 13), deleting ('took this back' in 13), search (12), media viewer (14).

Delivery state is honest rather than flattering. There are five states with five distinct marks (app/lib/spine/projections/thread.dart:12-27, app/lib/regions/chat/note.dart:300-357), the record and the paper use the same words, and a refusal is shown in red with the host's reason on the note instead of being hidden or silently re-pushed. The 13 report's `states_on_the_glass` matches what I read off the pixels.

The year is navigable without endless flinging: a search hit taps through to its place in the thread (app/lib/regions/chat/chat_region.dart:123 and 814, via ItemScrollController), and the search results in 12_search.png are ordered strictly newest-first (07:24, 07:20, 07:14, 11:52, 06:38 across 4 Aug, 10 Jun, 1 Apr) with the matched word highlighted in each.

Ordering is right everywhere I could check it. The six sampled frames of 11_chat_scroll run 22 Apr, 26 Apr, 26 Apr, 26 Apr, 27 Apr, 27 Apr with no reversal; the seeded year is 14,061 events with zero duplicate keys; reliability.json reports 174 events on both sides, 0 duplicates, same order both sides, seq 1..173 gapless after a scripted offline gap.

The held-frame accounting in frames.json is verifiable. I re-ran the three-term test myself on all 1,925 frames of the four clips (06: 310, 07: 421, 08: 518, 15: 376) and found zero held frames, matching `repeated_frames: 0` in every entry.

The stills flagged `from_this_run: false` in MANIFEST.json are not pictures of an older build, which I checked rather than assumed: the whole served bundle under app/build/web is dated 18:47-18:48 and nothing in it was rewritten afterwards, no .dart file under app/lib has changed since 18:31, and the earliest artifact was written at 18:49:20. The staleness is capture bookkeeping, not a stale build.

The two missing artifacts are missing for a reason rather than an excuse. 09_two_devices.png and 16_setup_android.png need an Android device; WHY_MISSING.json records that /dev/kvm is absent, that this was measured (adbd answered after 113 minutes with no framework behind it), that no GTK build was substituted and that nothing was faked from the PWA.

verdict: As a messenger this is far more complete than it has any right to be: twelve named capabilities and every one of them visible somewhere, five distinct delivery states with five distinct marks, a search that highlights its matches and taps through into a fourteen-thousand-event year, and a fling I could not fault — I measured all 299 transitions of 11_chat_scroll.mp4 against the app's own fling log and the pixels moved what was asked to within nine tenths of a device pixel, with no repeated, reversed or torn frame anywhere in 1,925 clip frames. What stops it clearing the floor is not sloppiness but two places where a person is left holding something the app will not carry, and one place where the evidence simply cannot answer the question. A note the far phone refuses stops for ever: it is marked honestly in red, and then there is no send-again in the menu and the outbox is coded never to try it again, so the only route is to retype it somewhere else — and one of the two refusal reasons is a pairing mismatch, which is a thing people fix and then expect to retry. Second, nothing here shows a message announcing itself to a closed app: the reception scene pushed three times and produced two byte-identical screenshots of an empty desktop and an empty records list, and its own note concedes the iPhone case appears nowhere in this build. Third, the scroll is the category's showpiece and the clip is taken on a driven clock, so it cannot drop a frame by construction; the one number that does speak to real time says a quarter of frames need six hundred and fifty to eleven hundred milliseconds of build, on a period that matches a new note entering the viewport. Alongside those sit smaller things that are still daily friction: the search chip covering thread text or a timestamp in 171 of 300 scrolled frames, every voice note in Moments undated behind a dangling separator because an int is handed to a date formatter that only parses strings, a 401 in the one scene the capture marked not-ok, and a first launch that takes up to twenty-six seconds behind no picture at all. Any one of the first two is a reason to open Instagram, which the row says caps this category at its floor; two of them, plus a states artifact that lost the typing indication it was written to capture and never shows the offline queue at all, puts it just under.
